title: Raga Gujri
hook: a quiet morning raga, devotion that doesn't announce itself

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Asa, So Dar, and your line was the dawn raga. Which doorway did you stop at, and what did you hear? Day one thousand seventy-four.

What does devotion sound like when nobody's watching? Not the big festival, not the packed hall. Something smaller. A grandmother who covers her head and murmurs a line before she lights the stove. A man who wipes down the steps of the gurdwara before anyone arrives and leaves before anyone thanks him. A teenager with one earbud in on the bus, listening to kirtan at low volume. None of it is loud. All of it is meant. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga with that temperament. Today: Raga Gujri.
screen: `DEVOTION WITH NO AUDIENCE.` → `SMALL, MEANT, UNSEEN.` → `RAGA GUJRI.`

segments.voice: Gujri comes after Asa in the Granth's order of ragas. Tradition places it in the morning, and its mood is usually described as quiet and devotional: not the forward lean of hope we heard in Asa, but something more settled, like someone who has already turned toward God and simply stays turned. The hymns gathered here come from several of the Gurus, and from Bhagats too. Here's a line from Guru Amar Das in Gujri, given in plain English: serve the Lord, and serve no other. It's short, and it doesn't raise its voice. That's a fair picture of the raga. Now, why would quiet devotion need its own music? Because a lot of devotion is quiet. Sikh practice has its great public moments, the processions, the gatherings, the langar lines. But it also lives in small repeated acts: reciting a bani in the morning, a whispered Waheguru, sweeping a floor. Gujri gives that side of faith a sound. It doesn't try to stir a crowd. It keeps company with one person. There's a second thing worth noticing. The raga is named in the shabad's own heading, so in the tradition of singing the Granth in its ragas, the text chooses the music, not the singer's mood that day. A shabad headed Gujri is set to be sung in Gujri. So the quiet is part of the instruction. The Guru set these words to be heard softly, and the music guards that. That's today's line: quiet devotion.
screen: `AFTER ASA, A SETTLED MOOD.` · `SERVE THE LORD, AND NO OTHER.` · `MUSIC FOR THE QUIET SIDE OF FAITH.` · `THE TEXT CHOOSES THE RAGA.` · then, large: `QUIET DEVOTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lower the volume. Sit, and let your shoulders come down. Breathe a little more softly than usual, as if someone nearby were asleep. Now think of one small thing you do faithfully that nobody notices: a call to a parent, feeding a pet on time, a glass of water for someone else. Let it count. You don't have to make it bigger. If you pray, you can whisper Waheguru once, as quietly as you can and still hear it. If you don't, let the quiet itself be enough. Later, play one Gujri shabad at low volume. The bell holds the time.
Raga Gujri. A raga tradition places in the morning, quiet and devotional, music for the faith that doesn't announce itself. Today's word.
Your line: quiet devotion. Today, do one kind thing without mentioning it to anyone, not even later. Day one thousand seventy-four.
